title: Illinois congressmen split on 'Big Beautiful Bill' - NewsBreak
text: PEORIA, Ill. (WMBD) — As Congress races to meet a self-imposed July 4th deadline for the sweeping reconciliation bill, Illinois lawmakers are clashing over its potential impact on communities that rely on Medicaid and SNAP benefits. U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.) said the so-called ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ will help working people, but his Democratic counterpart, U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen said it will do just the opposite, while devastating the communities they live in. “This Big Beautiful Bill is anything but beautiful. It’s ugly. It is horrific. It’s un-American. It hurts working families all while giving a tax break to billionaires,” said Sorensen. One in three people in the 17th Congressional District depend on Medicaid, Sorensen warned, and 64,000 people are set to lose their food assistance benefits. “This bill makes the single largest cut to health care and food assistance in the United States’ history. This bill is going to hurt Republicans and Democrats equally. This is going to be devastating to families who are struggling today, who don’t know how they’re going to make it,” he said. But LaHood doesn’t see it that way. “Focus on the middle class, no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on car loans, you know, tax on the elderly. Folks who rely on Social Security. This does a lot to help working-class people, but also to help the private sector,” he said. The bill cuts nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid. For a healthcare hub like Peoria, Sorensen said the ripple effects will cost lives and jobs, because states won’t be able to make up the difference. “If Medicaid reimbursements go down, it means that our hospital systems in Peoria may not be able to afford to have the oncologists that are going to be there to find the cancers. And it certainly means that smaller communities, like Canton or Galesburg, those areas are going to be even in more jeopardy because of the number of patients is so much lower there than it is in Peoria,” he said. LaHood said fears of losing benefits are overblown. He defended the bill, saying it protects vulnerable populations. “If you’re a working mother and you’re on Medicaid with young children, you get to keep your Medicaid benefits. If you’re a senior citizen who can only rely on Medicaid, you keep your Medicaid. If you have a child with developmental disabilities, you keep your Medicaid,” he said. If you can work and no longer qualify for Medicaid, LaHood said the government will help you find employment and become self-sufficent. “If you’re an able-bodied adult, we want you to get a job. If you’re in your 30s and 40s and 50s and you can work and you’re still on Medicaid, we’re going to try to transition you to work. We’re going to help you with work, training to get you into a job. We have seven million unfilled jobs in the country,” he said. Sorensen had some harsh words for his Republican counterpart. “Darin LaHood needs to look inside his soul and make sure that what he is voting on is going to do right with him. This is all about your legacy when you’re a member of Congress, that you’re trying to make the best decisions that you can for the most number of people,” he said. The reconciliation bill is expected to face a vote by Friday. Whether it passes may depend on lawmakers still struggling to get back to Washington after storms on the East Coast caused travel delays earlier in the week.
